title: Despite early start, Canada's flu season may be 'far from peak' as holidays approach

blocks.text: Health·New

Influenza appeared relatively early this fall, with a strain that often impacts younger adults. Medical experts aren't yet sure if this wave of infections will peter out before the holidays or if Canada will see a second surge of flu later in the winter.
H1N1 strain circulating now can impact young, healthy individuals, and second wave of infections also possible
An early start to Canada's flu season has medical experts bracing for a range of possibilities, from influenza-free holiday gatherings to the risk of a second wave later this winter.

The latest national data shows nearly 15 per cent of flu tests came back positive in the week ending Nov. 14, up from close to 14 per cent of tests the week before. Outbreaks and hospitalizations are also up, Public Health Agency of Canada figures show, with influenza A detected in almost all test samples.

Roughly four in 10 positive tests were among older adults aged 65 and up — one of the groups at the highest risk of serious illness — though the H1N1 strain circulating this year can actually be worse for younger adults and children.

"We're really on a concerning trajectory in terms of both the volume and the speed of [the] rise of the cases right now," said Dr. Lynora Saxinger, an infectious diseases specialist and professor at the University of Alberta.
"And by the numbers, I'm very concerned about how difficult it might get."
This flu season might be worse for young people
Rise in infections putting pressure on hospitals

Influenza appeared relatively early this fall — weeks before the country's past two seasons — with the west coast bearing the brunt of those initial infections. Flu cases began appearing in B.C. by early October, and in Alberta, roughly a quarter of all flu tests were coming back positive in early November.
The ongoing rise in cases is already putting pressure on at-capacity hospitals, said Saxinger, who is based in Edmonton.
"[This week] I was seeing people in an ambulance bay. Many have basically been there for days," she told CBC News.

blocks.text: It's a mixed bag elsewhere in the country, said Dr. Allison McGeer, a Toronto-based infectious diseases specialist with Sinai Health System.
"B.C. is probably close to the peak of the wave by now. The peak in Ontario and Quebec is probably going to be early to mid-December," she said.
"And then, hopefully, that's it."
But she acknowledged that an early end to flu season — before the holidays are fully underway — may be wishful thinking, given the unpredictability of influenza in any given year.
H1N1 strain can impact kids, young adults
Canada-wide, Saxinger said the season is likely "far from peak," with the potential for another surge of flu in the months ahead.

In some years, the virus rises and falls twice in the same season. Though H1N1 is dominant this fall, it's possible another strain could spike later in the winter, leading to a distinct second wave of infections.

blocks.text: "We have had recent years where things have been very strange and we've actually switched strains partway through," said Saxinger. "And it's also very common to have influenza B come up at the end."
What you need to know about this year's flu season in Ontario
Still time to get flu shot, experts say
The takeaway for Canadians? It's still worth getting a flu shot, even for young and healthy individuals.

Multiple experts agreed the early dominance of H1N1 this year could hit both kids and younger adults harder than usual, as many lack prior exposure to the similar virus strains that circulated decades ago among older generations.

"[B.C. has] seen a lot of emergency room visits, doctor's office visits; it's really gone up for young children, particularly zero to five, and then the young elementary age children," said Dr. Bonnie Henry, B.C.'s provincial health officer. "But we're not seeing it so much in adults yet."

blocks.text: Young adults who skipped the flu shot may have a higher risk of infection this year, Saxinger warned, though overall numbers still show more older adults testing positive.
"We will probably see a higher number of otherwise healthy people getting more severely ill this season," she said.
Flu season strikes Quebec early — and most people now have to pay for the shot
COVID, RSV seasons underway as well

COVID and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are also circulating at varying levels this fall, with the latest federal numbers showing more than six per cent of tests were recently coming back positive for COVID while less than one per cent of tests showed RSV.

After multiple severe RSV seasons in the wake of the COVID pandemic, McGeer said this "quieter than usual" year is giving the country a reprieve from a lesser-known infection that typically sends both the youngest and oldest into hospital.

blocks.text: With B.C.'s respiratory virus season the furthest along, Henry remains hopeful it won't be nearly as severe as other recent years given the relative lack of RSV cases. "We're happy that we're not having influenza and RSV at the same time," she added, "because that's where you really see the impact on … children's hospitals."

McGeer also stressed that highly effective vaccines and monoclonal antibody shots are available to protect against RSV — for infants, children, pregnant individuals and older adults — on top of the shots meant to ward off COVID and flu.
"This is going to be an 'everybody should take precautions' flu season," Saxinger said.
